think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 41-year-old male with pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis on ruxolitinib presents with subacute fever, productive cough, and marked CD4 T-cell lymphopenia, acutely complicated by syncope, lower extremity DVT, and pulmonary thromboembolism. Imaging reveals pulmonary infection, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and soft tissue encasement of the left main bronchus. The central diagnostic challenge is differentiating typical pyogenic pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, or disease-related extramedullary hematopoietic tumors from an opportunistic or paucibacillary mycobacterial infection masked by immunosuppression.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following initial emergency evaluation and stabilization of acute thromboembolic complications on Days 1-2, where chest CT demonstrates pulmonary infiltrates, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and peribronchial soft tissue thickening, prior to invasive bronchoscopy, bronchoalveolar lavage, and lymph node biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Bacterial pneumonia presents acutely with purulent sputum and leukocytosis but typically responds to empiric antibiotics and does not cause concentric peribronchial soft tissue masses or mediastinal lymph node necrosis. Pulmonary infarction accounts for infiltrates and pleural effusions in the setting of documented pulmonary embolism but cannot account for bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Extramedullary hematopoietic tumor or secondary lymphoma can produce mediastinal masses in myelofibrosis but yields cellular hematologic atypia rather than mycobacterial DNA on tissue biopsy.
case_prompt:
A 41-year-old male with a history of pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis (intermediate-1 risk by DIPSS, JAK2 V617F-positive, managed with ruxolitinib 20 mg twice daily for four months) presented to the hospital with a one-week history of fever and productive cough.

On physical examination, the abdomen was distended, and palpation revealed splenomegaly with the lower spleen edge extending to the level of the umbilicus. Breath sounds were decreased over the lung bases.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 16.11 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 40 mm/h, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 107.7 mg/L, and procalcitonin of 0.76 µg/L. Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets demonstrated marked cell-mediated immunodeficiency, with an absolute total T-cell count of 347/µL (normal reference range: 995–2860/µL) and an absolute CD4+ T-cell count of 208/µL (normal reference range: 550–1440/µL).

The morning after admission, the patient experienced a transient syncopal episode. Bedside venous ultrasound of the left lower extremity confirmed multiple deep venous thromboses. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed pulmonary thromboembolism involving the right upper and inferior pulmonary arteries, bilateral pleural effusions, pulmonary infiltrates, multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, and soft tissue shadows encircling the left main bronchus. Head CT also demonstrated an incidental frontal lobe hemorrhage.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the acute-to-subacute presentation of fever, productive cough, elevated procalcitonin, and pulmonary consolidation in an immunocompromised host. However, empiric antibacterial therapy failed to resolve the infection, and routine workup did not yield a conventional bacterial pathogen.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was hospitalized on 12th July for antibiotics.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pulmonary infarction secondary to acute pulmonary thromboembolism
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because the patient developed acute syncope, confirmed lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, and bilateral pulmonary emboli with pleural effusions and consolidative changes. However, thromboembolism alone could not explain the progressive mediastinal lymphadenopathy and soft tissue masses encasing the left main bronchus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Enhanced CT showed pulmonary thromboembolism in his right upper and inferior pulmonary artery, bilateral pleural effusion, pulmonary infection, multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes and soft tissue shadows that surrounded his left main bronchus

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Extramedullary hematopoiesis or secondary hematologic malignancy / lymphoma
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because patients with primary myelofibrosis and JAK2 mutations can develop extramedullary myeloid tumors, chloromas, or secondary lymphomas manifesting as mediastinal masses and lymphadenopathy. However, histopathologic and molecular evaluation of the lymph node demonstrated mycobacterial infection rather than malignant cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Given that infection work-up was negative, fiberoptic bronchoscopy was chosen to determine whether he was infected with TB.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Despite initial sputum smears being negative and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid testing negative for culture, AFB smears, and rapid molecular assays, a tracheobronchial lymph node biopsy ultimately confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis via polymerase chain reaction, establishing tracheobronchial tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A tracheobronchial lymph node biopsy finally confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) by polymerase chain reaction. He was diagnosed with tracheobronchial tuberculosis (TBTB)

editor_comments: Case represents tracheobronchial tuberculosis in a patient with primary myelofibrosis on ruxolitinib. All pathogen names, IGRA/T-SPOT, AFB smears, and invasive diagnostic biopsy results strictly excluded from case_prompt. Breakpoint set after initial emergency stabilization and CT imaging.
